appHelp.fragment.2: A spotlight walk through the table's controls, one at a time. Each tour ran once when you first sat down; take it again whenever you like.
appHelp.fragment.4: Create a campaign from the home page, or join a friend's with their invite code or a
appHelp.fragment.6: link. Build a character in the creation wizard, or reuse one saved to your library under Characters in the account menu. When everyone in the lobby is ready, the owner starts the adventure.
appHelp.fragment.7: If the server has campaign plugins installed, the create form also offers a
appHelp.fragment.9: to run the campaign in. See Campaign plugins below for what that changes.
appHelp.fragment.11: Before the game begins, each player readies up and whoever steers the story (the party lead, or the DM when a person runs the table) can adjust the game settings: genre, an optional secret story setup for the DM, dice policy, narration voice, and maps. Share the room code or copy the invite link to bring in more players; the owner or the DM opens the table once everyone is ready.
appHelp.fragment.13: The buttons above the message box change what your message means:
appHelp.fragment.15: Describe what your character does. The DM narrates the outcome and asks for dice rolls when the rules call for them.
appHelp.fragment.17: Speak in character. Your text is sent as spoken dialogue, in quotes.
appHelp.fragment.19: Out-of-character table talk. The DM does not respond to it, and it stays available even when the floor is locked during narration or a spotlight.
appHelp.fragment.21: Party lead only. Send the DM an authoritative story direction it must weave into the tale, or arm one of the seven canned events: Combat, Place, Social, Romance, Mystery, Weird or Windfall. Turn on
appHelp.fragment.23: and the direction goes to the DM alone: no character hears it, it never enters the transcript, and it steers the next turn instead of this one. The table still sees that something is armed, just never what.
appHelp.fragment.24: Questions are not one of these buttons. Open the
appHelp.fragment.26: strip just above the message box and use its own question box. Set
appHelp.fragment.28: to Auto, Story, Rules or My sheet to say where the answer should come from, and
appHelp.fragment.30: to Just me or The table to say who reads it. Answers quote what the campaign has on record under
appHelp.fragment.32: Asking writes nothing to the transcript and never moves the story on, so it works during narration, during someone else's spotlight, and while the floor is locked. Collapsing the strip keeps a half-typed question and your place in the thread.
appHelp.fragment.33: Sometimes the DM puts one player in the spotlight and waits for them to act. While the floor is locked for you, a banner explains why, and OOC and the Ask strip still work. Small chips above the message box name the background work the engine is doing between turns, such as compacting history, sealing a chapter, running the world tick or answering an Ask, with how long it has been going.
appHelp.fragment.35: While a fight is on, your options appear as a hand of cards above the message box: one for each weapon you carry, each spell you have prepared, your class features, and the basic actions (Dodge, Dash, Disengage, Help, Hide, Ready, Grapple, Shove, Use an object, End turn). Each card shows what it costs (action, bonus action, reaction, a spell slot, a use) and what it rolls, worked out from your sheet.
appHelp.fragment.36: Pick a card, pick who it lands on from the chips or by tapping them on the battle map, check the line under
appHelp.fragment.38: , then press the gold button named after the card.
appHelp.fragment.40: puts that line in the message box so you can change it first. A dimmed card is spent for the turn; hover or press it to see why. Rider cards such as Divine Smite attach to your next attack.
appHelp.fragment.41: The hand never replaces typing. The message box, Do, Say and OOC, the microphone and Enter to send all work exactly as before, and the arrow on the hand's bar puts it away. The question mark beside it replays the two-line introduction.
appHelp.fragment.42: When the DM gets it wrong
appHelp.fragment.43: Hover a DM message and a row of actions appears above it. None of them advance the story or change a single number the rules produced. Rewriting the narration belongs to the party lead, since everyone reads the same transcript:
appHelp.fragment.45: lead only. Have the DM write that moment again with the same dice and the same outcome, optionally with a note on what to do differently. Only the prose changes.
appHelp.fragment.47: lead only. Once a second version exists, arrows and a counter appear in the message header. Paging between takes swaps the message for the whole table.
appHelp.fragment.49: lead only. Have the DM keep writing from where a reply stopped short, without moving the story on.
appHelp.fragment.51: lead only. Fix what the DM said by hand. Mechanics are untouched and every dice marker in the passage has to survive the edit.
appHelp.fragment.53: anyone. Flag the passage, or just the text you selected, against the campaign record and see whether it contradicts anything already established.
appHelp.fragment.54: If a DM turn fails outright, a banner offers to send it back in from where it stopped. It resumes the turn that was already running, so nobody has to retype an action and nothing lands in the transcript twice.
appHelp.fragment.56: Recent turns are in front of the DM word for word. Older ones are compacted into a rolling summary, and closed chapters become chapter summaries it can search and re-read when the table brings up something from long ago.
appHelp.fragment.58: any player can select text in a DM message and press the bookmark icon, or press it with nothing selected to keep the whole message. Pinned memories ride in every prompt from then on. There is a size budget, and the Pinned memories list under Story, Facts shows how much of it the table has spent.
appHelp.fragment.60: party lead only, because it writes to the campaign record. Keeps a passage in front of the DM permanently as established fact.
appHelp.fragment.62: Story, Facts also holds DM secrets the DM must never contradict and the lore entries the table has written up.
appHelp.fragment.64: under Party, where each character stands with the people they have dealt with.
appHelp.fragment.65: NPCs the party stops mentioning are archived so they do not crowd out the ones in play, and the party lead can see exactly what the DM was sent on the last turn, plus anything the budget cut, in the Context tab.
appHelp.fragment.68: the roster, with character sheets, HP and conditions for the whole party, and the active encounter during combat. A Bonds sub-tab appears when relationships are on. The room code is in the lead's tab.
appHelp.fragment.70: the tactical battle map, while a fight with a map is running. Move your token on your turn.
appHelp.fragment.72: the scene map, the overworld and discovered locations, when maps are enabled.
appHelp.fragment.74: three sub-tabs. Chapters is the tale so far and the arc in play, and it is where you export the story. Facts holds pinned memories, DM secrets and lore. Log is the audited record of every dice roll and every stat change the DM makes.
appHelp.fragment.76: suggest campaign notes for the story; the party lead approves them.
appHelp.fragment.78: private whispers between you and the DM, and side chat between players that the DM and the campaign transcript never see.
appHelp.fragment.80: party lead only. What the DM was actually sent last turn, and anything the token budget dropped.
appHelp.fragment.82: campaign settings, invites and game toggles.
appHelp.fragment.84: Every check, save, and attack is rolled by the server, never invented by the AI. The dice button in the header opens
appHelp.fragment.86: : tap dice into the tray (or type an expression such as 2d6+3), add a bonus, and roll. Turn on
appHelp.fragment.88: to roll behind the screen: a DM's secret roll is seen by the DM seats alone, and a player's by that player and the DM; the rest of the table is not told a die was rolled. The same menu toggles the 3D dice animation. If you opt into real dice in the game settings, the DM waits for you to enter your physical roll, with a digital fallback button if you would rather let the server roll.
appHelp.fragment.89: Once you have opted in, the
appHelp.fragment.91: button in the Party tab lets you decide per die which happens: type the physical roll yourself, let the server roll that die for you, or read it straight from a connected
appHelp.fragment.93: . Pairing a Pixel needs a Chromium-based browser and a secure (https) connection, because that is what Web Bluetooth requires. When every die in a request is covered by a Pixel or the server, the roll submits itself the moment the last die lands. These choices are saved in the browser you set them in, so set them again if you switch devices.
appHelp.fragment.95: When narration is enabled, the DM reads its replies aloud. Use the speaker button in the header to unmute (browsers require one click before audio can play) and the slider to set the volume. Hover a DM message to replay its narration. Push-to-talk, when configured, lets you hold the microphone button to dictate your message.
appHelp.fragment.97: When the server and the campaign both have voice chat switched on, a
appHelp.fragment.99: card appears in the lobby, and during play a
appHelp.fragment.101: sits in the top bar with the full voice menu under it. Join and you are talking to the table; no other app needed, and the call stays up whatever panel you switch to. The microphone needs a secure (https) connection, and your browser will ask permission the first time.
appHelp.fragment.102: Whoever runs the story can open
appHelp.fragment.104: for a split party or a private word, and can hold the floor: soft enforcement marks who should be talking, strict actually mutes everyone else, and a raised-hand queue keeps it civil. A table can also opt into rules that make the call behave like the world: proximity hearing (you only hear players whose characters are near yours on the map, while the DM hears everyone), whisper and shout ranges, walls muffling speech, and downed characters going deaf. All of that lives under voice settings in Setup, and all of it is off by default, so a plain group call is what you get until the table asks for more.
appHelp.fragment.106: With ambience enabled in the game settings, the table shares a soundtrack: a background bed for where the party is (a tavern, a forest, a crypt), a music layer for what the scene is doing, and one-shot stings for dramatic moments. The DM changes it as the story moves, and combat brings its own sound. Whoever runs the story can also hold a layer on a chosen cue so the auto-picker leaves it alone. Your speaker button and volume slider in the header control it for you alone, and it ducks automatically while narration speaks.
appHelp.fragment.107: The sounds themselves are public-domain and Creative Commons recordings the server admin installs; see the licenses page for who made what. If ambience is on but silent, the server simply has no audio installed yet.
appHelp.fragment.109: A campaign does not have to be run by the AI. Created with
appHelp.fragment.110: a person in the DM seat
appHelp.fragment.111: , the table works the way a kitchen-table game does: the DM narrates in their own words (most tables do it over voice chat), and the app keeps the sheets, the dice, the maps and the record straight underneath them. Your Do and Say messages still land in the transcript, but instead of waking the AI they queue as intents for the DM to answer. The DM holds no party slot (though they can build a companion to play from the console), holds the story secrets the party lead would hold at an AI table, and gets a console of tools: initiative, monsters, maps, NPCs, roll tables and rulings, with an AI assistant one click away for stat blocks and suggestions if they want it.
appHelp.fragment.114: , lets the DM keep the story and hand the bookkeeping to the AI a piece at a time: it can run the monsters' turns, read the DM's notes aloud as full prose, or
appHelp.fragment.116: for a counted stretch of answers while the DM steps away, following the outline they left behind.
appHelp.fragment.117: Because the narration happens out loud, the app nudges the DM every so often to jot down a
appHelp.fragment.119: , a line or two about what just happened. Beats are what chapter summaries, recaps and the exported story are built from, so a table that never writes any ends up with a transcript of intents and no tale. Players can help by keeping their actions in the composer rather than only in the call.
appHelp.fragment.121: The campaign owner starts as party lead and can pass the role from a party member's menu. The lead steers the table: the Direct message mode with its event presets and private directions, approving suggested notes, releasing a stuck spotlight, retrying a halted turn, rerolling or editing a narration, letting new players join mid-game, and editing campaign settings and house rules.
appHelp.fragment.122: The lead also owns the story spine, under Story, Chapters. A single beat can be reworded, skipped or promoted to the one in play without regenerating the whole arc, a chapter can be sealed early, and the whole campaign can be rewound to the start of a chapter. A rewind is destructive: it asks for confirmation and lists what it will undo first, then puts sheets, NPCs, locations, maps and quest state back the way they were.
appHelp.fragment.123: Where the engine spots two NPC names that might be the same person but refuses to merge them on a guess, the lead is the one who settles it.
appHelp.fragment.124: At a table with a human DM the split is different: the lead keeps the invites and the campaign details but is otherwise a player, because the story powers listed above exist to steer the AI and there is no AI to steer. Story secrets, settings, rules, floor control, narration fixes and the DM seats belong to the person in the DM seat instead.
appHelp.fragment.126: A campaign can run in a
appHelp.fragment.128: : a pre-built setting with its own races, classes, spells, gear, monsters, factions and lore, and a brief telling the DM how that world should sound. Picking one at creation also sets the campaign's genre and can fill in its theme and premise.
appHelp.fragment.129: A pack renames things, it never changes a rule. Everything underneath is still 5e, your sheet still stores the canonical names, and a character built in a pack campaign can be brought into a plain one and simply reads under its ordinary names again.
appHelp.fragment.130: Server admins install and remove packs under Admin, Campaign plugins, from a registry or from a file. A pack built on somebody else's setting carries an unofficial-work notice wherever it appears: it is fan-made and is not affiliated with, sponsored by or endorsed by the rights holder.
appHelp.fragment.132: You do not need to know the rules to play; the DM and the server handle them. When a term comes up that you do not recognize, look for the small info button next to it: every feature, spell and stat on your sheet explains itself.
appHelp.fragment.135: collects the basics in plain language and lets you search every spell, feat, item and condition the app knows about. The
appHelp.fragment.137: is the whole fifth edition reference document, searchable, for the moment a rule needs checking word for word. Its contents are bound as three books: the players' rules, the Dungeon Master's, and the monsters, each holding everything the reference document opens from the Player's Handbook, the Dungeon Master's Guide and the Monster Manual (the rest of those books is not openly licensed). At the table it opens from the book button in the header.
appHelp.fragment.139: Open Dungeon Master is a self-hosted, multiplayer Dungeons & Dragons 5e platform run by an AI Dungeon Master. Server admins manage users, models, images, voice and campaign plugins from the Admin panel. Game content comes from the SRD 5.1 and Open5e; see

workshopHelp.copy.m050: A spotlight walk through the controls, one at a time. Each tour ran once when you first opened its page; take it again whenever you like.
workshopHelp.copy.m052: What each tool is for, how a first session with it goes, and the things people miss.
workshopHelp.copy.m053: The tool you have open comes first.
workshopHelp.copy.m055: A prep space: everything a campaign holds, with no players, no transcript and no AI narrator. Build the material on your own time, then bring it into a real campaign when the table sits down. Nothing you do here can start a fight or move a story, because there is no story running. The stand-in party bar at the top sets the party size and level your prep is measured against, so encounter difficulty readouts mean something before real characters exist.
workshopHelp.copy.m056: Into a campaign, and back out
workshopHelp.copy.m059: step: pick a workshop (or another campaign you can see) and choose what to copy in. A campaign lobby can import the same way after creation. Copies are copies: the workshop keeps its version, the campaign owns its own from then on, and name collisions get numbered instead of overwritten. The Share tool exports the whole workshop as a bundle file another server can import, and can compile a draft world pack from it.
workshopHelp.copy.m061: A whole workshop can be cloned from the shelf or the hub, and individual pieces (maps, NPCs, monsters, encounters, tables, lore) each have a duplicate action, for the version-two-of-this-boss workflow. Homebrew monsters, items, spells and options belong to your account rather than to any one workshop. The Share tool can include your whole shelf or just the entries this workshop uses; imported conflicts get their own names instead of changing your existing rules.
workshopHelp.copy.m063: Everything here is still 5e underneath: attack expressions have to roll, challenge ratings show their working, and imported material behaves in a campaign exactly like material made there. When you want the numbers themselves, the rules reference and its calculators are one click away in the account menu.
workshopHelp.guide.world.title: WorldForge
workshopHelp.guide.world.purpose: The world itself, after Smoebo's WorldForge: a wiki of typed entries, the web of links between them, calendars and a timeline, an atlas, secrets, and the names still to write.
workshopHelp.guide.world.step.0: Open a WorldForge file, or make a first entry: pick its type and name it. It lands in the Cast, Places, Factions or Lore, by its type.
workshopHelp.guide.world.step.1: Open the entry to write its article, fill its type's fields, and add the hidden truth only you know.
workshopHelp.guide.world.step.2: Add links: pick the other entry from the list, choose the words, and say whether it is common knowledge, a hidden truth or a false belief.
workshopHelp.guide.world.step.3: Add a calendar and the events of the world's history, naming who and where.
workshopHelp.guide.world.step.4: Write the secrets and who keeps them, and mark each learned when the party finds out.
workshopHelp.guide.world.step.5: Read the world for names still to write, and save it back out as a WorldForge file when you like.
workshopHelp.guide.world.tip.0: Every entry is the same row the Cast, Region, Factions and Lore tools edit: change it in either place.
workshopHelp.guide.world.tip.1: The AI DM is told each NPC's hidden truth, ties and secrets, and the secrets the party has not learned, never to state them outright.
workshopHelp.guide.world.tip.2: Choose What people believe in the web to see the world as the players will hear it.
workshopHelp.guide.world.tip.3: With a text model, Forge turns notes into entries and links, Ask answers from the world, and Draft writes an entry's text; with an image backend, Paint makes its picture. Without them those tools are simply not offered.
workshopHelp.guide.storyboard.title: Storyboard
workshopHelp.guide.storyboard.purpose: The plan of the adventure as cards: scenes, fights, places, people and payoffs.
workshopHelp.guide.storyboard.step.0: Pick a card kind and give it a title, then Add.
workshopHelp.guide.storyboard.step.1: Open a card to write it up and link it to an NPC, a map, a prepared fight or a place from the dropdowns.
workshopHelp.guide.storyboard.step.2: Use Leads to on a card to chain it to the cards that follow.
workshopHelp.guide.storyboard.step.3: Read What this board is missing and add the cards it suggests.
workshopHelp.guide.storyboard.step.4: Check What this becomes: it is what the board turns into when imported into a campaign.
workshopHelp.guide.storyboard.tip.0: Links are dropdowns over the other tools, so build the NPC or the map first and the card can point at it.
workshopHelp.guide.storyboard.tip.1: The missing list is counted, never guessed by a model.
workshopHelp.guide.party.title: Party
workshopHelp.guide.party.purpose: The stand-in party the prep is measured against, and the pregens that travel with it.
workshopHelp.guide.party.step.0: Set the size and level in the bar at the top of the workshop and Save.
workshopHelp.guide.party.step.1: Pick a character from your library and Add it, or Build a new one.
workshopHelp.guide.party.step.2: Take one off with the cross; it stays in your library.
workshopHelp.guide.party.tip.0: A pregen whose level differs from the stand-in party is flagged on its card.
workshopHelp.guide.party.tip.1: Pregens ride along inside the bundle when you share the workshop.
workshopHelp.guide.maps.title: Battle maps
workshopHelp.guide.maps.purpose: Rooms to fight in, drawn, rolled or imported, with lights, doors, labels and props.
workshopHelp.guide.maps.step.0: Open New map, name it, and choose Roll one, Blank rock, Blank ground or Import .dd2vtt.
workshopHelp.guide.maps.step.1: Tap the map in the drawer to open the editor.
workshopHelp.guide.maps.step.2: Paint with the brush, line, outline, box and fill tools; undo is there when a stroke goes wrong.
workshopHelp.guide.maps.step.3: Place lights, doors, labels and props with their tools; a bystander prop offers the cast as a dropdown.
workshopHelp.guide.maps.step.4: Set the theme, ambient light, tags and notes, and the sound the map makes.
workshopHelp.guide.maps.step.5: Put it on the table when a campaign is running, or open it as a scene.
workshopHelp.guide.maps.tip.0: Nothing here touches a table until you put it there.
workshopHelp.guide.maps.tip.1: A backdrop picture hangs behind the grid, so a hand-drawn map still gets the engine's lighting and doors.
workshopHelp.guide.maps.tip.2: Tags you have used on other maps are offered as a dropdown beside the tag field.
workshopHelp.guide.region.title: Region
workshopHelp.guide.region.purpose: The overworld: the land, roads, rivers, borders, labels and the places on it.
workshopHelp.guide.region.step.0: Pick a mode (Add pin, Paint terrain, Draw a line, Write a label) and tap the map.
workshopHelp.guide.region.step.1: Under Shape the region, describe the land in a sentence to set the dials, or Roll a world.
workshopHelp.guide.region.step.2: Add places by name so NPCs, cards and fights can point at them.
workshopHelp.guide.region.step.3: Use a picture instead of tiles, read in an Azgaar map, or save the region as a PNG.
workshopHelp.guide.region.tip.0: Players see a place only once the party has discovered it.
workshopHelp.guide.region.tip.1: Regenerate rerolls the terrain; places keep their spots where the new ground allows.
workshopHelp.guide.encounters.title: Encounters
workshopHelp.guide.encounters.purpose: Fights prepared in advance and budgeted against the stand-in party.
workshopHelp.guide.encounters.step.0: Open How hard is this? to weigh a roster before saving it: pick monsters from the search, then Work it out.
workshopHelp.guide.encounters.step.1: Press New encounter. Name it and pick monsters into the roster; edit the counts in the box below.
workshopHelp.guide.encounters.step.2: Choose the map it opens on, then place each creature and the party's entrance on it.
workshopHelp.guide.encounters.step.3: Write the plan: what the fight is worth, and what happens when.
workshopHelp.guide.encounters.step.4: Prepare it. At the table the fight is one press of Deploy.
workshopHelp.guide.encounters.tip.0: The difficulty pill is the same maths the engine enforces; every number in the workbench shows its parts.
workshopHelp.guide.encounters.tip.1: A monster the world does not know is flagged on the card rather than failing at the table.
workshopHelp.guide.cast.title: Cast
workshopHelp.guide.cast.purpose: The people of the world, with personalities, goals and relationships.
workshopHelp.guide.cast.step.0: Press Someone new. Give them a name, a role and an attitude to the party.
workshopHelp.guide.cast.step.1: Pick where they are found from the places the world has, or type a new one.
workshopHelp.guide.cast.step.2: Fill in who they are underneath, what they want, and how they feel about the others.
workshopHelp.guide.cast.step.3: Save them, then add a face: upload one or have one painted.
workshopHelp.guide.cast.tip.0: Suggest fills a single field from a text model, when the server has one.
workshopHelp.guide.cast.tip.1: Set aside hides someone without deleting them; the cast also fills itself in as the party meets people.
workshopHelp.guide.bestiary.title: Bestiary
workshopHelp.guide.bestiary.purpose: Your own monsters as full stat blocks the engine can run.
workshopHelp.guide.bestiary.step.0: Open Build a monster. Name it and pick a challenge rating, or find a catalogue monster to start from.
workshopHelp.guide.bestiary.step.1: Open the block. Set abilities, attacks and traits; Saves from scores fills the saves for you.
workshopHelp.guide.bestiary.step.2: Use Build it out of the catalogue to take size, hit points, armour and attacks from an ancestry, class and gear.
workshopHelp.guide.bestiary.step.3: Add spells known from the catalogue search, languages from the dropdown, and where it is found.
workshopHelp.guide.bestiary.step.4: Save the block. The rating is derived and shows its working.
workshopHelp.guide.bestiary.tip.0: Monsters belong to your account, not the workshop, so they follow you everywhere. The Share tool can include your whole shelf or just the entries this workshop uses.
workshopHelp.guide.bestiary.tip.1: Put a round of casting into extra damage so the rating counts it.
workshopHelp.guide.homebrew.title: Homebrew
workshopHelp.guide.homebrew.purpose: Items, spells, feats, backgrounds, species and subclasses of your own.
workshopHelp.guide.homebrew.step.0: Pick the kind at the top, then press New.
workshopHelp.guide.homebrew.step.1: Start from something in the books: search the content pack and copy a row in.
workshopHelp.guide.homebrew.step.2: Change what you like. Skills, languages, conditions and damage types are dropdowns you can also type into.
workshopHelp.guide.homebrew.step.3: Read the findings under the description; an error blocks saving.
workshopHelp.guide.homebrew.step.4: Keep it. The character builder and the engine read it like the books' own.
workshopHelp.guide.homebrew.tip.0: A spell's damage, save and damage type are read out of its description, the way the SRD's are.
workshopHelp.guide.homebrew.tip.1: Everything is checked against the ruleset as you type.
workshopHelp.guide.lore.title: Lore
workshopHelp.guide.lore.purpose: The world bible: places, factions, history and secrets the narrator treats as canon.
workshopHelp.guide.lore.step.0: Press New entry. Pick a category and a title.
workshopHelp.guide.lore.step.1: Write the entry in Markdown. Link another entry from the dropdown; the link lands at the cursor.
workshopHelp.guide.lore.step.2: Choose whether the table reads it or only you do.
workshopHelp.guide.lore.step.3: Attach a picture to make it a handout, add tags, and Add.
workshopHelp.guide.lore.step.4: Pin the entries the narrator should see every turn.
workshopHelp.guide.lore.tip.0: Unpinned entries are retrieved by relevance, so a long bible costs nothing until it is needed.
workshopHelp.guide.lore.tip.1: Tags already in use are offered beside the tag field.
workshopHelp.guide.tables.title: Tables
workshopHelp.guide.tables.purpose: Random tables: rumours, treasure, weather, encounters, anything rolled.
workshopHelp.guide.tables.step.0: Press New table and name it.
workshopHelp.guide.tables.step.1: Write one row per line, with a range (1-3) or a weight (x3), or paste a table from a book.
workshopHelp.guide.tables.step.2: Use the picker under the box to add a row that is a thing: another table, a monster, an item, a person or a lore entry.
workshopHelp.guide.tables.step.3: Watch the coverage line for gaps and overlaps.
workshopHelp.guide.tables.step.4: Save table. Roll from the card; Draw without replacement makes it a deck.
workshopHelp.guide.tables.tip.0: Rolling writes an ordinary roll everyone can see, but what the row says comes back to you alone.
workshopHelp.guide.tables.tip.1: Look up a monster beside the tables is a catalogue stat block for reference.
workshopHelp.guide.rules.title: Rules
workshopHelp.guide.rules.purpose: Variant rules the engine honours and house rules the narrator retrieves.
workshopHelp.guide.rules.step.0: Toggle the variant rules and set the rest length.
workshopHelp.guide.rules.step.1: Write house rules grouped by heading, and Save rules.
workshopHelp.guide.rules.step.2: Switch a section off to silence it, or pin it to include it every turn.
workshopHelp.guide.rules.step.3: Save these rules as a ruleset to reuse in other campaigns and workshops.
workshopHelp.guide.rules.step.4: Apply a saved ruleset here; the preview says what changes first.
workshopHelp.guide.rules.tip.0: Applying a ruleset copies it; editing it later never reaches back.
workshopHelp.guide.plugin.title: Plugin
workshopHelp.guide.plugin.purpose: A world pack of your own: the setting's names over the rules, its lore, and its pictures, as one file any server can install.
workshopHelp.guide.plugin.step.0: Run Guided setup: name the world, say what it is inspired by and who owns that, pick the base genre, and write the narrator's brief.
workshopHelp.guide.plugin.step.1: Pull from this workshop to bring in the lore, places, hook cards and cast you already built.
workshopHelp.guide.plugin.step.2: In People, Magic and gear, and Bestiary, pick the thing from the catalog and give it the world's name for it.
workshopHelp.guide.plugin.step.3: In Pictures, upload a cover and a picture for any race, class, monster, place or faction; they are resized to fit on the way in.
workshopHelp.guide.plugin.step.4: Open Publish. Fix what it lists, then Download the pack, or Install it here if you run this server.
workshopHelp.guide.plugin.tip.0: A pack renames; it never changes a rule. Anything mechanical is a homebrew entry, not a pack.
workshopHelp.guide.plugin.tip.1: Fill in the rights holder for anything built on somebody else's setting; it turns the notice into a proper disclaimer.
workshopHelp.guide.plugin.tip.2: The draft travels inside the workshop bundle, so sharing the workshop shares the half-built pack too.
workshopHelp.guide.share.title: Share
workshopHelp.guide.share.purpose: The whole workshop as one file, or compiled into a draft world pack.
workshopHelp.guide.share.step.0: Name the bundle and say what it is in a line.
workshopHelp.guide.share.step.1: Fill in the author and version; add the rights holder if it is built on somebody else's setting.
workshopHelp.guide.share.step.2: Download bundle, or Compile a world pack.
workshopHelp.guide.share.tip.0: Pictures travel with the bundle within the size caps; nothing from any campaign does.
workshopHelp.guide.share.tip.1: Hand-built monsters and homebrew belong to your account. Choose the whole shelf or only the entries this workshop uses when exporting a bundle.
